name: Zion National Park
tagline: Navajo sandstone walls, a river you hike up, and a shuttle that runs the show

hero.alt: Zion Canyon at sunrise with the Virgin River below towering red and cream sandstone walls

quickFacts.label: Entrance fee
quickFacts.note: $30 motorcycle, $20 per person on foot or bike

quickFacts.label: Reservation to enter?
quickFacts.note: Only Angels Landing and wilderness routes need permits

quickFacts.label: Best months
quickFacts.note: Warm days, cool nights, a river you can wade

quickFacts.label: Shuttle season 2026
quickFacts.note: Plus December 26 – January 2; free, no ticket

quickFacts.label: Time zone
quickFacts.note: All permit deadlines are quoted in MT

overview.summary:
Zion is a narrow, 2,000-foot-deep gash of Navajo sandstone with a river running through the bottom, and almost everything famous about the park happens inside that one canyon. The two signature hikes go straight at the geology: Angels Landing climbs a fin to a knife-edge strung with chains, and The Narrows abandons dry land and walks you upstream between walls you can touch on both sides.

Know this first: from March 7 to November 28, 2026 you cannot drive Zion Canyon Scenic Drive. A free shuttle runs it every 5–10 minutes, nine stops, no ticket. The rest of the park — the Zion–Mount Carmel Highway, Kolob Canyons, Kolob Terrace Road — stays open to cars all year, and is where you go when the canyon feels full.
dontMiss: Riding the shuttle to Temple of Sinawava and walking the Riverside Walk into the mouth of the Narrows
Canyon Overlook Trail east of the tunnel — an hour for the best view-to-effort ratio in the park
Court of the Patriarchs at low sun, when Abraham, Isaac and Jacob light up
Angels Landing, if the lottery goes your way and heights don't
The Zion–Mount Carmel Highway east to Checkerboard Mesa

alerts.text: East Rim Trail is partially closed by rockfall near Weeping Rock. Hidden Canyon is closed, and Observation Point cannot be reached from Zion Canyon — the only route is the East Mesa Trail from the east side.

Toxic cyanobacteria health watch on the Virgin River and park streams (updated 2026-05-21). Do not submerge your head, touch algae mats, or drink or filter in-stream water — no recreational filter removes cyanotoxins. Children and dogs are most at risk. Wading is still allowed.

Since June 7, 2026, large vehicles are banned from the Zion–Mount Carmel Highway between Canyon Junction and the East Entrance — anything over 35 ft 9 in long, 7 ft 10 in wide, 11 ft 4 in tall or 50,000 lbs is turned around at the gate. This replaced the old tunnel-escort permit, so ignore older advice about buying one.
South Campground reopened May 29, 2026 after rehabilitation. Reservations are required and open only 14 days ahead.
The Narrows closes when the Virgin River runs above 150 cubic feet per second and during any Flash Flood Warning. Check flow and the flash flood potential rating the morning you go.

seasons.name: Spring
seasons.notes: The sweet spot for temperature and the worst stretch for the Narrows: snowmelt pushes the river past the 150 cfs closure line, and NPS warns it "may be closed for an extended period of time." Nights stay cold — the daily swing can be 32°F or more — and March and April are wet. Crowds arrive fast: March draws almost three times February's visitors, the shuttle goes full-time March 7, 2026, and South Campground reopens.

seasons.name: Summer
seasons.notes: Hot and crowded — "regularly over 100°F," 16 days above 100°F in an average July, roughly half a million visitors a month, parking often full by 9:00 am. The upside is the Narrows: flow drops to wadeable and water reaches 56–68°F. The downside is the monsoon, July–September, with 14–15 thunderstorm days a month and real flash-flood risk. Hike at dawn and carry a gallon per person.

seasons.name: Fall
seasons.notes: The other sweet spot, and better than spring if the Narrows is your reason for coming — flow is low and the water still tolerable in September. September stays busy (11% of the year's visitors) before visitation drops sharply in November. Daily swings of 30°F are normal, and color shows at the highest elevations by late October. The shuttle's last run drops to 5:00 pm from October 25.

seasons.name: Winter
seasons.notes: The quiet season, and the only time you can drive the Scenic Drive yourself — the shuttle stops after November 28 and returns only December 26 to January 2. Expect 13–20 freezing nights a month and snow that "typically disappears within a matter of hours at lower elevations." Ice on the Angels Landing chains and the Riverside Walk is the real hazard; Kolob Terrace Road and often Kolob Canyons Road close with snow.

gettingThere.how: The usual approach. I-15 north into Utah, then UT-9 east through Hurricane and La Verkin to Springdale and the South Entrance.
49 miles via I-15 north to UT-9 east. Full-size groceries are here, and it is a common budget base.
60 miles. Convenient if you want Kolob Canyons first — that entrance is at I-15 Exit 40, only 17 miles south of Cedar City.
300 miles, essentially all I-15 south. Most people break the drive.

Enter at the East Entrance, 13 miles west of Mt. Carmel Junction on SR-9, and drive the Zion–Mount Carmel Highway down into the canyon. NPS gives the alternate route via Highway 20 north of Cedar City as roughly 150 miles and 2.5 hours. Large vehicles cannot use this route since June 7, 2026.

logistics.gettingAround:
From March 7 to November 28, 2026, and again December 26 to January 2, personal vehicles are barred from Zion Canyon Scenic Drive. The free Zion Canyon Line runs it with nine stops — Visitor Center, Human History Museum, Canyon Junction, Court of the Patriarchs, Zion Lodge, The Grotto, Weeping Rock, Big Bend, Temple of Sinawava — every 5–10 minutes, about 45 minutes end to end. Only Zion Lodge and Canyon Trail Rides guests with reservations, and medical accommodation permit holders, may drive it.

The free Springdale Line runs nine stops through town every 10–15 minutes to the park's Pedestrian/Bike Entrance. Park in town and ride in: the visitor center lot holds just over 350 cars and NPS says parking "often fills by early or mid-morning" February through November. Everything east of Canyon Junction, plus Kolob Canyons and Kolob Terrace Road, stays open to cars year-round.
logistics.fees: $35 per private vehicle, $30 per motorcycle, $20 per person on foot or by bicycle (16+); standard passes are valid 7 days. A Zion Annual Pass is $70. America the Beautiful is $80 for residents and $250 for non-residents; Senior Annual $20, Senior Lifetime $80, Military and Access passes free. No charge for either shuttle. 2026 fee-free days: Feb 16, May 25, Jun 14, Jul 3–5, Aug 25, Sep 17, Oct 27, Nov 11.

permits.name: Angels Landing permit
permits.how: Everyone hiking past Scout Lookout needs one, via recreation.gov only. A seasonal lottery runs months ahead; a day-before lottery opens 12:01 a.m. and closes 3 p.m. MT with results at 4 p.m. MT. Cost: $6 per application (up to six people, non-refundable) plus $3 per person if awarded, refundable if you cancel two or more days out on a seasonal permit. Your start time is measured at The Grotto and rangers check anywhere on the trail. The 2026 seasonal lotteries ran Feb 13–25, Apr 1–20 and Jul 1–20; the one for Dec 1, 2026 – Feb 28, 2027 opens October 1, 2026.

permits.name: The Narrows bottom-up
permits.how: No permit. You can walk upstream from the Temple of Sinawava as far as Big Spring without one. The limits are the river, not paperwork: the route closes above 150 cfs and during Flash Flood Warnings.

permits.name: The Narrows top-down / overnight
permits.how: The 16-mile through-hike from Chamberlain's Ranch needs a wilderness permit, as does any overnight campsite in the Narrows. Three routes to a day permit: an advance reservation on recreation.gov at least a day ahead, a daily lottery two days before (12:00 a.m.–3:00 p.m. MT), or first-come, first-served at the Wilderness Desk the day before. Day use is $6 per application plus $10 per person per day; overnight is $20 per reservation plus $7 per person per night. Arrange your own ride to Chamberlain's Ranch.

permits.name: Canyoneering permits
permits.how: Required for every canyon needing ropes or descending gear. Advance reservations open up to three months ahead and stay bookable until 5:00 p.m. MT the day before; a daily lottery runs two days out (12:00 a.m.–3:00 p.m. MT), and walk-in spaces go the day before at the Wilderness Desk. Fees: $6 per application plus $10 per person.

permits.name: Wilderness / backpacking permit
permits.how: Needed for all overnight backpacking, climbing bivouacs, Narrows and tributary through-hikes, and all trips into the Left Fork of North Creek. $20 per reservation plus $7 per person per night. Permits are picked up in person by the reservation holder at the Visitor Center Wilderness Desk and are non-transferable. Campfires are prohibited in the Zion Wilderness.

logistics.reservations: You do not need a reservation or timed entry to enter Zion, and you do not need one to ride the shuttle — NPS states both plainly. The only things you reserve are an Angels Landing permit, a wilderness or canyoneering permit, a campsite, or a room. Camping is the tight one: Watchman books six months out and the park says campgrounds are "full almost every night mid-March through late November."
logistics.services: Open 24 hours a day, year-round. Zion Canyon Visitor Center 8 am–5 pm, Human History Museum 10 am–5 pm, Kolob Canyons Visitor Center 8 am–12 pm and 1 pm–5 pm; rangers answer 435-772-3256 from 10 am to 5 pm MT. Zion Lodge is the only place inside the park to buy food, and holds the gift shop and post office. Water and restrooms are at the visitor center, The Grotto, Scout Lookout and the Riverside Walk trailhead. Groceries, fuel, restaurants and the outfitters renting Narrows gear are in Springdale. Cell coverage is unreliable in the canyon — download maps first.

attractions.name: Angels Landing
attractions.permitNote: Required for everyone past Scout Lookout, via recreation.gov only. $6 per application (up to six people) plus $3 per person if awarded. Apply in the seasonal lottery months ahead, or in the day-before lottery — 12:01 a.m. to 3 p.m. MT, results at 4 p.m. MT. Start time is measured at The Grotto. No permit is needed to reach Scout Lookout.
attractions.bestTime: First shuttle at 7:00 am — the switchbacks face the sun and the chains bottleneck by mid-morning
attractions.seasonNote: Chains and slickrock ice up in winter; the route stays open with a permit, but traction devices matter
attractions.summary: The park's signature hike, and one of the most exposed maintained trails in the national park system. The West Rim Trail climbs the canyon wall in paved switchbacks, cools off in Refrigerator Canyon, then stacks 21 tight switchbacks — Walter's Wiggles — to Scout Lookout. From there a half-mile fin runs to the summit along a ridge under three feet wide in places, chains bolted into the rock, drop-offs of up to 1,000 feet.
tips: Hike to Scout Lookout without a permit — great view, and you decide about the chains there
Skip the chains if the rock is wet or icy or the wind is up; there is no easy retreat mid-ridge
Fill up at The Grotto — no water past it, and restrooms end at Scout Lookout
attractions.accessibility: Not accessible. Unpaved, rocky, under 3 ft wide in places; not for young children. Pets prohibited

attractions.name: The Narrows (bottom-up)

stats.distance: Any length; up to 10 mi round trip
stats.elevationGain: Negligible — you walk upstream in the riverbed
stats.time: 2 hr for a taste; all day to Big Spring
stats.trailheadOrParking: Temple of Sinawava (shuttle stop 9), then 1 mi on the Riverside Walk

attractions.permitNote: No permit going upstream from the Temple of Sinawava as far as Big Spring. A wilderness permit is required only for the 16-mile top-down through-hike from Chamberlain's Ranch, or to camp.
attractions.bestTime: Late summer and early fall, when flow is low and the water is warmest
attractions.seasonNote: Often closed for weeks during spring snowmelt; closes above 150 cfs and in any Flash Flood Warning
attractions.summary: There is no trail — the Virgin River is the route. You wade, sometimes thigh-deep, up a slot where the walls close to a couple of dozen feet apart and rise a thousand. No permit is needed, which is why it is also the most crowded hike in the park. Most people go an hour or two upstream and turn back; Big Spring is a ten-mile round trip and a full day.
tips: Check flow and the flash flood rating that morning — 150 cfs closes it
Rent canyoneering boots, neoprene socks and a stick in Springdale
56–68°F in summer but 41–53°F spring and fall; dress for hypothermia, not a swim
attractions.accessibility: The paved Riverside Walk to the river's edge is accessible; the Narrows is not

attractions.name: Riverside Walk
attractions.bestTime: Early morning or the last shuttle up — the walls glow and the crowd thins
attractions.seasonNote: Can close in winter when the pavement ices over
attractions.summary: The paved path at the end of the shuttle line, following the river upstream while the canyon squeezes shut. Hanging gardens seep from the walls, and the trail ends where the river fills the canyon floor — the doorway to the Narrows. Nearly everyone who rides the shuttle walks it, and it earns the traffic.
tips: Ride to the last stop first thing; queues here are worst mid-day
Stop where the pavement ends even if you skip the Narrows — that is the view
Restrooms and water are at the trailhead and nowhere beyond
attractions.accessibility: Concrete, typically 77 in wide at about a 4.6% grade — wheelchair and stroller friendly, with some irregular paving and minor drop-offs

attractions.name: Emerald Pools

stats.elevationGain: 333 ft to Middle; 76 ft more to Upper
stats.trailheadOrParking: Emerald Pools Trailhead across from Zion Lodge (shuttle stop 5), or The Grotto (stop 6) via the Kayenta Trail

attractions.bestTime: Spring, when the ephemeral waterfalls are actually falling
attractions.seasonNote: Open year-round; the waterfalls are seasonal and can be dry by late summer
attractions.summary: The classic family hike from Zion Lodge, and three destinations you can take as far as you like. Lower runs under a dripping overhang behind a thin waterfall; Middle climbs a sandstone ledge to open canyon views; Upper ends at a green pool in a dead-end amphitheater below the Great White Throne.
tips: Up the Kayenta Trail from The Grotto, down to Zion Lodge, and it becomes a loop
Do not enter the pools — fragile wildlife water, and swimming is prohibited
The pools are on the cyanobacteria advisory list; keep dogs and children out
attractions.accessibility: Lower is partly paved but rough; Middle and Upper are unpaved with steps and ledges

attractions.name: Canyon Overlook Trail

stats.trailheadOrParking: Small lot on SR-9 immediately east of the Zion–Mount Carmel Tunnel — drive yourself, no shuttle

attractions.bestTime: Sunrise or the hour before sunset; the lot is emptiest at dawn
attractions.seasonNote: Drivable and hikeable all year, but the slickrock and the steps are slick when wet or icy
attractions.summary: The best view in Zion per unit of effort. A half-mile of sandstone steps, handrails and a catwalk bolted over a dark slot canyon opens onto red and cream slickrock, ending at a fenced cliff edge above the switchbacks of the Zion–Mount Carmel Highway, with the Towers of the Virgin beyond.
tips: NPS says it plainly: "Parking is extremely limited, be prepared to try multiple times"
East side, outside the shuttle system — you need a car to get here
Do it driving out toward the East Entrance in low afternoon light
attractions.accessibility: Not accessible — steps, uneven rock, tread narrowing to 12 in, drop-offs. Pets prohibited

attractions.name: Zion Canyon Scenic Drive & Court of the Patriarchs

stats.distance: Nine shuttle stops end to end
stats.time: About 45 min one way; about 1.5 hr for a full round trip without getting off

attractions.permitNote: No permit, but no private cars either during shuttle season — March 7 to November 28, 2026, and December 26 to January 2. Only Zion Lodge and Canyon Trail Rides guests with reservations, and medical accommodation permit holders, may drive it.
attractions.bestTime: The first shuttle at 7:00 am, or the last runs of the evening for low light
attractions.seasonNote: Drivable in your own car only outside shuttle season, and it closes for the day when its parking fills — common in December, January and February
attractions.summary: The spine of the park, and what almost every visitor actually does. The shuttle runs the canyon floor past the Court of the Patriarchs, Zion Lodge, The Grotto, Big Bend and the Temple of Sinawava, walls rising 2,000 feet on both sides. Court of the Patriarchs at stop 4 is the set-piece: a short steep walk to an overlook facing Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, named in 1916.
tips: Shuttles come every 5–10 minutes — get off freely, you are never stranded long
Ride to stop 9 first, then work back down; the crowd moves the other way
Court of the Patriarchs faces east: brilliant in the morning, flat by afternoon
attractions.accessibility: Every shuttle bus is wheelchair accessible (lift limit 600 lbs; chairs to 45 in long by 25 in wide). The Court of the Patriarchs overlook walk is short but steep

attractions.name: Zion–Mount Carmel Highway & Checkerboard Mesa

stats.elevationGain: Climbs out of the canyon in a series of engineered switchbacks
stats.trailheadOrParking: Canyon Junction (SR-9) — open to private vehicles year-round

attractions.permitNote: No permit. Since June 7, 2026 large vehicles are prohibited here: nothing over 35 ft 9 in long, 7 ft 10 in wide, 11 ft 4 in tall or 50,000 lbs, and combined vehicles no more than 50 ft with a trailer under 26 ft. Oversize vehicles are turned around at the entrance stations.
attractions.bestTime: Late afternoon heading east, when the slickrock warms up
attractions.seasonNote: Open all year; snow and ice are possible on the switchbacks in winter
attractions.summary: Opened July 3, 1930, this is the road that made the Grand Circle tour of Zion, Bryce and the Grand Canyon possible: switchbacks stacked up the canyon wall, a long tunnel bored through the cliff, and a different landscape beyond. East of the tunnel the red canyon gives way to cream slickrock domes, ending at Checkerboard Mesa, cross-hatched into a giant grid.
tips: Pull into every signed overlook; Checkerboard Mesa has its own near the East Entrance
The drive to do when shuttle queues are absurd — it needs no shuttle
Bighorn sheep are common here; slow down and do not approach
attractions.accessibility: Fully drivable; the overlooks are roadside pullouts with short, mostly level approaches

attractions.name: Pa'rus Trail

stats.trailheadOrParking: Zion Canyon Visitor Center (shuttle stop 1) or Canyon Junction (stop 3)

attractions.bestTime: Sunset, then stay for the stars
attractions.seasonNote: Open and usable year-round, including when the shuttle is not running
attractions.summary: "Pa'rus" is Paiute for bubbling water, and the trail follows the river from the visitor center to Canyon Junction on pavement and boardwalk, with the best straight-on views of the Watchman in the park. It is Zion's only pet-friendly trail and its only bike trail, which makes it far more useful than its easy rating suggests.
tips: The one trail where leashed dogs are allowed — leash no longer than 6 feet
Bikes allowed, so it is the natural link from Springdale to Canyon Junction
Sunset over the Watchman from the bridges is the classic Zion photograph
attractions.accessibility: 93.6% paved with the remainder hardwood decking, minimum tread width 96 inches, typical grade 2.6% — wheelchair accessible

attractions.name: Watchman Trail

stats.trailheadOrParking: Zion Canyon Visitor Center — walk through the plaza past the shuttle stop

attractions.bestTime: Late afternoon into sunset, when lower Zion Canyon turns orange
attractions.seasonNote: Year-round, but muddy or icy in winter and in the monsoon, with very little shade in summer
attractions.summary: The best short hike you can start without touching a shuttle. It runs flat along the river, then climbs sandy switchbacks to a bench below the Watchman, with a loop at the top over lower Zion Canyon, the temples and towers, and Springdale. The obvious answer when you arrive mid-afternoon and the shuttle line is 40 minutes long.
tips: Perfect first-evening hike — you can walk to the trailhead from Springdale
Almost no shade; in summer go after 5 pm, not at noon
No bikes and no pets on this one
attractions.accessibility: Not accessible — sandy, rocky, uneven, with moderate drop-offs

attractions.name: Observation Point via East Mesa Trail

stats.trailheadOrParking: East Mesa Trailhead, reached only by high-clearance or 4WD dirt roads off North Fork Road

attractions.permitNote: No permit — but Observation Point can no longer be reached from Zion Canyon. The East Rim Trail from Weeping Rock is partially closed by rockfall, and the East Mesa approach is the only way there.
attractions.bestTime: Morning, before the mesa bakes and before afternoon storms build
attractions.seasonNote: Roads can be "extremely muddy and inaccessible in the winter, spring, and after rainstorms"
attractions.summary: Observation Point sits roughly 700 feet above Angels Landing and looks down on it, and the East Mesa Trail gets you there almost level — you start high on the plateau and walk to the rim instead of climbing out of the canyon. The catch is access: a rough dirt road, no shuttle, no services. The best big overlook in Zion per unit of suffering, and no lottery.
tips: Check the road first — a passenger car is not enough, and mud shuts it for days
Park only in designated spaces; illegally parked vehicles are cited or towed
Carry all your water; there is nothing at this trailhead
attractions.accessibility: Not accessible; the trailhead is not reachable by ordinary vehicles

alsoConsider.name: Kolob Canyons & Timber Creek Overlook
alsoConsider.why: A separate entrance at I-15 Exit 40, 40 miles from Zion Canyon and 17 miles south of Cedar City: a five-mile scenic drive under 2,000-foot crimson walls, no shuttle at all. Timber Creek Overlook is 0.6 mi each way with 117 ft of gain. The road can close in winter.

alsoConsider.name: The Subway (Left Fork of North Creek)
alsoConsider.why: Zion's other lottery. Bottom-up is a very strenuous 9-mile round trip with knee-deep water and boulder scrambling; top-down is a 9.5-mile technical through-hike needing rappelling skills, 60 feet of rope and swims through deep pools. A wilderness permit is always required, group size is capped at 12, and both a seasonal and a daily lottery run on recreation.gov.

alsoConsider.name: Kolob Terrace Road & Lava Point
alsoConsider.why: The high, quiet third of the park, climbing out of Virgin, UT into ponderosa country about an hour from Zion Canyon. Lava Point has six primitive campsites and a big overlook. Usually closed fall through spring for snow.

camping.name: Watchman Campground
camping.where: Just inside the South Entrance, next to the Zion Canyon Visitor Center and the Pedestrian Entrance. Walk to the shuttle stop, and walk into Springdale for dinner.
camping.bookingDetail: 100% reservation — no first-come, first-served sites. Standard sites open on recreation.gov six months in advance, and the park says campgrounds are "full almost every night mid-March through late November." Five loops: A and B electric (30-amp, a few 50-amp), tents or RVs; C and D non-electric, barring vehicles 19 feet or over including combined length; E tent-only group sites for 7–40 people; F walk-to, tent-only. No hookups beyond power and no water or sewer at sites, but a dump station with potable water sits at the entrance ($5 for non-campers). Sites take 6 people, 2 vehicles, 3 tents; check-out 11 am, check-in after 12 pm, quiet hours 10 pm–8 am.
camping.goodFor: Tents and RVs in A/B; non-electric C/D loops cap vehicles at 19 ft
camping.imageAlt: Watchman Campground below the Watchman peak

camping.name: South Campground
camping.where: Also near the South Entrance, within walking distance of the visitor center, the shuttle and Springdale.
camping.bookingDetail: Reopened May 29, 2026 after a full rehabilitation — no longer closed. Reservations are required on recreation.gov and open only 14 days before arrival, a short sharp window that makes it a real option for trips you did not plan six months out. Closes for winter. Unlike Watchman, generators are allowed, 8–10 am and 6–8 pm only.
camping.sites: Varies — the park has not published a post-rehabilitation site count
camping.goodFor: Tents and smaller RVs; the fallback when Watchman is full

camping.name: Lava Point Campground
camping.where: High on Kolob Terrace Road, roughly an hour from Zion Canyon — cool, forested, and removed from the canyon scene.
camping.bookingDetail: Six primitive sites, reservable on recreation.gov up to 14 days in advance. There is no water — bring everything. Closes seasonally, and Lava Point Road is typically closed fall into spring. It cannot be part of a wilderness backpacking itinerary. Generators 8–10 am and 6–8 pm.
camping.season: Seasonal; road typically closed fall into spring
camping.goodFor: Tents and small vehicles; escaping the canyon heat

lodging.name: Springdale, UT
lodging.distance: At the South Entrance — the park boundary is the north end of town
lodging.summary: A single main street running up to the park gate, and where the overwhelming majority of Zion visitors sleep — several dozen hotels, motels, inns and B&Bs in a town of barely 600 people. The decisive feature is the free town shuttle: nine stops the length of town, every 10–15 minutes, same season as the park shuttle, ending at the park's Pedestrian/Bike Entrance. Stay anywhere in town and you reach the park without moving your car. Springdale also has the groceries, restaurants, fuel and the outfitters renting Narrows gear; town parking is paid, with large-vehicle spaces.
lodging.imageAlt: Springdale, Utah, at the mouth of Zion Canyon

lodging.name: Zion Lodge
lodging.distance: Shuttle stop 5, in the middle of Zion Canyon
lodging.summary: The only lodging inside the park: 76 hotel rooms, 6 suites and 40 historic cabins on the canyon floor at shuttle stop 5, with the Emerald Pools and Kayenta trailheads across the road. It is also the only place inside the park to buy food — Red Rock Grill year-round plus a seasonal café — and holds the gift shop and post office. Guests with reservations are among the few allowed to drive the Scenic Drive in shuttle season. Rooms open roughly a year ahead and popular dates vanish immediately: zionlodge.com.

lodging.name: Nearby towns: Hurricane, La Verkin, St. George, Cedar City, Kanab
lodging.distance: Hurricane and La Verkin on the UT-9 approach; St. George 49 mi; Cedar City 60 mi; Kanab east of the park
lodging.summary: Hurricane and La Verkin are the standard budget answer — chain motels, RV parks and supermarkets directly on the UT-9 approach, so you are not detouring, just sleeping earlier on the same road. St. George (49 mi) has the deepest hotel supply; Cedar City (60 mi) is the practical base if you want Kolob Canyons first, 17 miles south at I-15 Exit 40. Kanab is the east-side base for a loop with Bryce Canyon and the North Rim — but check your vehicle size, since June 7, 2026 large vehicles cannot use that route. The tradeoff everywhere is arriving with the morning traffic rather than walking in ahead of it.

safety.title: Heat
safety.body: July averages 100°F with 16 days over 100°F, and June and August are barely cooler. NPS is specific: "Carry enough water, at least one gallon per person per day, and drink it" — and eat with it, because water alone does not replace salt. Start at first light and be off exposed rock by late morning. Heat exhaustion looks like nausea, headache, cramps and cool clammy skin: stop, find shade, elevate the feet, take fluids and food. Heat stroke is an emergency.

safety.title: Flash floods
safety.body: Flash floods happen year-round and peak with the monsoon — July and August average 14 and 15 thunderstorm days. They arrive as sudden surges carrying tree trunks and boulders, and a storm miles away can trigger one under blue sky. The park posts a daily flash flood potential rating: not expected, possible, probable, expected. Check it and the river flow before any slot canyon or the Narrows, which closes above 150 cfs and in any Flash Flood Warning. If water rises or muddies, get high — do not run downstream.

safety.title: Falls
safety.body: NPS states it directly: "Falls from cliffs on trails have resulted in death." Angels Landing is the sharpest example — press tallies compiled in 2021 counted 13 deaths in falls on Angels Landing and its approach since 2000, most on the final chained section; the park publishes no running total. The mechanics are ordinary: loose sand on slickrock is slippery, the ridge narrows to under three feet with 1,000-foot drops, and two-way traffic forces passing in bad places.

safety.title: Cold water and hypothermia in the Narrows
safety.body: The Narrows is a cold-water hike even in July: 56–68°F in summer, 41–53°F spring and fall, 38–45°F in winter, and you are in it for hours with little sun. NPS calls hypothermia "the number one killer of outdoor recreationists, even in summer" and a greater hazard in narrow canyons. Wear quick-drying layers, never cotton; rent neoprene socks and canyoneering boots spring and fall, a wetsuit or drysuit in winter. Carry a stick — the riverbed is slick, uneven and invisible.

safety.title: Toxic cyanobacteria in the Virgin River
safety.body: A health watch advisory is in effect (updated 2026-05-21) for the North Fork of the Virgin River — the Narrows, Pine Creek, Deep Creek, Kolob Creek, Orderville Canyon, the Emerald Pools — plus North Creek and La Verkin Creek. Do not touch or ingest algae mats, do not submerge your head, and do not drink in-stream water: no recreational filter removes cyanotoxins. Children and dogs are most at risk. Wading is not prohibited.

safety.title: Rockfall
safety.body: Rockfall is an ongoing hazard throughout Zion, especially near cliff faces — the 2019 rockfall near Weeping Rock still has the East Rim Trail partially closed and Hidden Canyon shut. Do not linger under overhangs or at the base of cliffs, and never throw or roll rocks. If rockfall starts and you cannot move clear, shelter behind a large boulder and pull your pack over your head. Keep your distance from wildlife too: NPS warns that contact with animals or their droppings can transmit dangerous illnesses.

safety.title: Winter ice
safety.body: Zion Canyon gets 13–20 freezing nights a month December through February, and nearly half the year's precipitation falls December through March. Canyon-floor snow melts fast, but ice persists on shaded slickrock, on the Angels Landing chains, and on the paved Riverside Walk, which can close when it glazes over. Traction devices are worth the space.

plan.what: Park in Springdale or at the visitor center and be at the stop before the first bus at 7:00 am. In summer the lot is often full by 9.
Ride to Temple of Sinawava (stop 9), about 45 minutes end to end. You arrive with the canyon almost to yourself.
Walk the Riverside Walk, 1 mile of pavement to where the canyon closes in. With boots and a stick, continue upstream into The Narrows for an hour or two — check flow and the flash flood rating first.

Back to Zion Lodge (stop 5) for the Emerald Pools: 2.2 miles and 333 feet to Middle, 0.3 miles each way more to Upper. Return via the Kayenta Trail for a loop, and eat at the lodge — the only food in the park.
Ten-minute stops at Court of the Patriarchs (stop 4) and Big Bend (stop 8), then shuttle out and collect the car.
Drive the Zion–Mount Carmel Highway east through the tunnel into white slickrock domes, ending at Checkerboard Mesa.
Hike Canyon Overlook, 1 mile round trip from the small lot east of the tunnel. Parking is extremely limited; late afternoon gives the best odds and the best light.
Dinner in Springdale, then the Pa'rus Trail for sunset on the Watchman and, once dark, the stars. Paved, flat, no shuttle needed.

Be on the 7:00 am first shuttle to The Grotto (stop 6). With an Angels Landing permit this is the morning — the chains jam by mid-morning. Without one, take the same West Rim Trail to Scout Lookout: 1.9 miles and 1,187 feet each way, no permit, most of the view.
Refill at The Grotto and take the Kayenta Trail across to the Emerald Pools, finishing at Zion Lodge for a late lunch.
Shuttle down, stopping at Court of the Patriarchs and the Human History Museum for the park film and the Towers of the Virgin.
Watchman Trail straight from the visitor center — 3.3 miles, 479 feet, about 90 minutes — for sunset over lower Zion Canyon. No shuttle required.

First shuttle to Temple of Sinawava, then the Riverside Walk and The Narrows properly: four to six hours upstream and back gets you well past Wall Street, and starting early buys quiet water and time to spare.
Dry off and eat in Springdale, then pick up the car. The afternoon belongs to the east side.
Drive the Zion–Mount Carmel Highway out to Checkerboard Mesa and back, stopping at the pullouts. Watch for bighorn sheep.
Canyon Overlook Trail at golden hour — 1 mile round trip for the view onto the highway switchbacks and lower Zion Canyon.
With a third morning, leave the canyon: Kolob Canyons off I-15 Exit 40, five-mile scenic drive plus the Timber Creek Overlook Trail. No shuttle, rarely crowded.

faq.q: Do I need a reservation to enter Zion?
faq.a: No. NPS states it plainly: "You do not need a permit or reservation to enter the park" and "You do not need a permit or reservation to ride a park shuttle." You do pay the entrance fee — $35 per vehicle, valid 7 days. The only reservations in play are Angels Landing permits, wilderness and canyoneering permits, campsites and rooms.

faq.q: Can I drive Zion Canyon Scenic Drive?
faq.a: Not during shuttle season. In 2026 the shuttle runs March 7 through November 28 plus December 26 to January 2, and personal vehicles are barred throughout; the exceptions are Zion Lodge and Canyon Trail Rides guests with reservations and medical accommodation permit holders. Outside those dates you can drive it — though the road closes for the day once its parking fills, common December through February. Everything east of Canyon Junction, plus Kolob Canyons and Kolob Terrace Road, is drivable all year.

faq.q: How do I get an Angels Landing permit?
faq.a: Only through recreation.gov, in one of two lotteries. The seasonal lottery runs months ahead for a three-month block; the one covering December 1, 2026 to February 28, 2027 opens October 1, 2026, closes October 20, permits issued October 25. Otherwise the day-before lottery opens 12:01 a.m. and closes 3 p.m. MT, results at 4 p.m. MT the same day. Either way: $6 per application for up to six people plus $3 per person if you win. No permit is needed to reach Scout Lookout, which is most of the climb and much of the view.

No minimum age, and plenty of families do the first mile or two — but be honest about conditions: you are wading a moving river over slick, uneven, invisible cobbles in water that is 56–68°F at its warmest and 41–53°F spring and fall, and current knee-deep on an adult is waist-deep on a child. Rent proper boots and a stick, go in late summer or early fall when flow is lowest, turn around early, and keep heads out of the water. If in doubt, the Riverside Walk gets the same scenery with none of it.

In 2026, March 7 to November 28, then a holiday run December 26 to January 2. The first bus leaves the visitor center at 7:00 am all season (8:00 am over the holidays). Last departure up-canyon is 6:00 pm Mar 7–May 16, 7:00 pm May 17–Sep 12, 6:00 pm Sep 13–Oct 24 and 5:00 pm Oct 25–Nov 28; the last bus down from Temple of Sinawava runs about 75 minutes later. Every 5–10 minutes in the canyon, 10–15 in Springdale. Free — no ticket, no reservation.

Yes — open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, and the only time you can drive the Scenic Drive yourself. Highs run 54–59°F with 13–20 freezing nights a month, and canyon-floor snow usually melts within hours. The catches: ice on the chains and shaded slickrock, Riverside Walk closures, Kolob Terrace Road closed and Kolob Canyons Road frequently closed, South Campground and Lava Point shut, and the Scenic Drive closing for the day when its parking fills. Watchman stays open year-round.

The visitor center lot has just over 350 spaces and the Human History Museum 51, and NPS says parking "often fills by early or mid-morning" February through November — in summer often by 9:00 am. The reliable move is to park in Springdale, which has paid street and lot parking including large-vehicle spaces, and ride the free town shuttle to the Pedestrian Entrance. If you must park inside, arrive before 8 am or after 4 pm, and prefer weekdays.

trip.title: Zion — the week before Thanksgiving, 2026
trip.pitch: Three nights in Springdale (plus a Las Vegas night on the way in) with Zion Canyon a mile up the road. Late November means cool, quiet trails, a shuttle that is still running, and the last week before the holiday crowds. There is room for more people: here is where we’ll be, when, and what’s worth coming for.

base.name: Springdale, UT
base.detail: We are staying in town, within 1 mile of the park’s South Entrance. Springdale sits right at the gate: restaurants, groceries, gas and Narrows gear rental are all on the one main street, and the free town shuttle stops along it and drops at the park’s pedestrian entrance, so we can leave the cars parked most days.
base.bookingNote: Book a Springdale room for Sun Nov 22, Mon Nov 23 and Tue Nov 24 (check out Wed Nov 25) — three nights, not four — as close to the South Entrance as you can, or ask about sharing ours. Add Las Vegas for Sat Nov 21 if you’re driving up with us. Springdale fills for the holiday week, so book early; see Stay for the town and example properties.
base.imageAlt: Springdale’s main street with Zion’s cliffs behind it

trip.arrival:
Sat Nov 21: drive up from Southern California and sleep in or near Las Vegas.
Sun Nov 22: Las Vegas → Springdale, about 170 mi, roughly 2 h 45 min via I-15 north and UT-9 east through Hurricane. Utah is on Mountain Time, one hour ahead of Las Vegas. Stop for groceries in Hurricane; Springdale has a small market.
trip.departure: Wed Nov 25: a short morning in the park, then the drive home. It is the day before Thanksgiving, so expect heavier I-15 traffic near Las Vegas by late afternoon.

conditions.label: Weather
conditions.text: November averages a 64°F high and 37°F low on the canyon floor, and about ten November nights drop below freezing. Great hiking days; mornings and evenings need layers.

conditions.label: Daylight
conditions.text: About ten hours. Sunrise is a little after 7 a.m. and the canyon is in shadow well before the ~5:15 p.m. sunset, so we start early and eat dinner in town.

conditions.label: Shuttle
conditions.text: The Zion Canyon shuttle runs through Nov 28: first bus 7:00 a.m., last bus into the canyon 5:00 p.m., last bus out 6:15 p.m. Private cars cannot drive the Scenic Drive while it runs. The free Springdale town shuttle runs the same season and drops at the park’s walk-in entrance.

conditions.label: Angels Landing
conditions.text: The Sep–Nov seasonal lottery closed in July, so the route in is the day-before lottery: apply between 12:01 a.m. and 3 p.m. Mountain Time (Utah is one hour ahead of Las Vegas) the day before you want to hike, $6 per application for up to six people, $3 per person if drawn. Scout Lookout — most of the climb and the view — needs no permit.

conditions.label: The Narrows
conditions.text: Open unless the river runs above 150 cubic feet per second (the park’s closure line) or a flash flood warning is issued. Water will be in the low 40s °F — rented dry pants or a drysuit from a Springdale outfitter is the difference between fun and misery. There is also an active toxic-algae advisory on the Virgin River: wading is fine, keep your head out and don’t drink or filter the water (details in Safety).

conditions.label: Is late November a good time?
conditions.text: It is a week past the Overview’s “best months” — we’re trading a little warmth for far fewer people, an empty shuttle, and low golden light on the walls. Visitation drops sharply in November; the holiday surge starts after we leave.

bring: Layers for 35–65°F: warm base layer, fleece or puffy, wind shell, beanie and gloves for mornings
Real hiking shoes with grip; microspikes if the forecast turns cold (shaded slickrock ices)
Headlamp — the canyon is dark by 5:30 p.m.
2 liters of water per person per hike; there is water at the visitor center and Zion Lodge
Recreation.gov account set up in advance for the Angels Landing day-before lottery
Narrows day: rent dry pants or drysuit, neoprene socks, canyon boots and a walking stick in Springdale; bring a dry bag
America the Beautiful pass if anyone has one ($35 per vehicle otherwise, good 7 days)
Snacks and a packed lunch — there is no food in the canyon beyond Zion Lodge

join.text: The more the better: hikes are more fun in a group, cars fill up efficiently, and dinners in Springdale are better with company. Come for the whole stretch or just a day or two.
steps: Coordinate with Aaron — which nights, how many people, and whether you’re driving or want a seat.
Book a Springdale room for Nov 22–24, or ask about sharing ours.
Set up a recreation.gov account so you can enter the Angels Landing day-before lottery with us.
Tap Add to my picks on what you’d want to do, then send Aaron the link — that’s how we plan cars and shuttle times.

cost.label: Springdale room, 3 nights
cost.note: The main cost; Thanksgiving week is peak. The Stay tab lists example properties to price.

cost.label: Park entrance
cost.note: Good for 7 days; split among the car. Free with an America the Beautiful pass.

cost.label: Angels Landing lottery
cost.note: $6 per application (up to six people), $3 per person only if you win.

cost.label: Narrows gear rental
cost.note: Dry pants or drysuit, boots and a stick from a Springdale outfitter, by the day — only if you do the Narrows.

trip.costNote: No group fee. Gas and entrance split per car; cars fill up, so ask Aaron for a seat.

keyDates.what: Book your Springdale room (Nov 22–24) — holiday-week rooms go first.
12:01 a.m.–3 p.m. Mountain Time: apply to the Angels Landing day-before lottery for Monday’s hike on recreation.gov ($6 per group). Results by 4 p.m. Repeat Monday for a Tuesday attempt.

faq.q: Roughly what will this cost me?
faq.a: Your Springdale room is the big number and depends on the property; the park is $35 per car for the week, the Angels Landing lottery is $6 plus $3 a person if you win, and Narrows gear is a day rental if you go. The rest is gas and food.

faq.q: Can I come for just one day?
faq.a: Yes. The best single day is Monday or Tuesday: first shuttle at 7 a.m., one big hike, dinner in town.

faq.q: Do I have to do Angels Landing?
faq.a: No. The chains section is exposed and needs a lottery permit. Scout Lookout, right below it, needs no permit and has most of the view. The Narrows, Emerald Pools, Canyon Overlook and the Watchman are all great days without it.

Very, for the right hikes: Pa’rus Trail (paved), Riverside Walk, the lower Emerald Pools, Canyon Overlook. In November keep kids to the first stretch of the Narrows. Angels Landing is not for young children.

faq.q: How fit do I need to be?
faq.a: If you can walk a few miles with some uphill, you have a full trip. Angels Landing to Scout Lookout is the steep one (about 1,200 ft of climb over 2 miles); the Narrows is slow wading, not climbing; several of the Top 10 are flat.
